source_lines.51: **Given:** AC; a field $k$, $G=\mathrm{SL}_2$ with diagonal torus $T_2$, upper triangular Borel $B=T_2\ltimes U^+$, root groups $U^+=\{\binom{1\ a}{0\ 1}\}$ and $U^-=\{\binom{1\ 0}{a\ 1}\}$, and a prime $p=\operatorname{char}(k)>0$ in the last part.
source_lines.53: [F1] *Root coordinates of $\mathrm{SL}_2$.* $X(T_2)=\mathbb Z\chi$, $\Phi=\{\pm2\chi\}$, $\alpha=2\chi$, $\alpha^\vee=\chi^\vee$ with $\langle\chi,\alpha^\vee\rangle=1$, the Weyl group is $\{1,s_\alpha\}$ acting by $s_\alpha(\chi)=\chi-\langle\chi,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha=-\chi$, $u_\alpha(a)=\binom{1\ a}{0\ 1}$, $u_{-\alpha}(a)=\binom{1\ 0}{a\ 1}$, and $\mathrm{SL}_2$ is generated by $U^+$ and $U^-$ ([[lem-sl2-structure-and-root-coordinates|Structure of $\mathrm{SL}_2$ and root coordinates]], [[def-root-datum-of-a-split-reductive-group]]).
source_lines.75: 1.1 With the identification $X(T_2)=\mathbb Z\chi$ of [F1], the fundamental weight is $\omega=\chi$ and $X(T_2)^+=\{m\chi:m\ge0\}$, so [F2] gives the simple modules $L(m)=V(m\chi)$ for $m\ge0$. The trivial representation is one-dimensional hence simple with highest weight $0$, so $L(0)$ is the trivial representation. The standard representation $k^2$ is simple: for any nonzero $v=(a,b)$ one has $\binom{a\ 0}{b\ a^{-1}}e_1=v$ when $a\ne0$ and $\binom{0\ -b^{-1}}{b\ 0}e_1=v$ when $a=0$, so the submodule generated by any nonzero vector is all of $k^2$; moreover $e_1$ is fixed by $U^+$ and is a $T_2$-eigenvector of weight $\chi$, so $e_1$ is primitive of weight $\chi=\omega$ and $k^2\cong L(1)$ by [F2]. [F1, F2]
source_lines.77: 1.2 Fix $m\ge0$ and let $v\in L(m)$ be a primitive vector of weight $m\chi$, which exists and is unique up to scalar by [F3]. By [F4] $L(m)$ is generated as a $U^-$-module by $v$, and $U^-=U_{-\alpha}\cong\mathbf G_a$. By [F5] write $u_{-\alpha}(c)\cdot v=\sum_{i\ge0}c^iv_i$, where $v_0=v$, $v_i\in L(m)_{(m-2i)\chi}$, and only finitely many $v_i$ are nonzero. Let $W=\operatorname{span}_k\{v_i:i\ge0\}$. For every $k$-algebra $R$ and $a\in R$, the group law gives $u_{-\alpha}(a)\cdot(u_{-\alpha}(c)\cdot v)=u_{-\alpha}(a+c)\cdot v$; comparing coefficients of $c^j$ in these polynomial expressions yields $u_{-\alpha}(a)\cdot v_j=\sum_{i\ge j}\binom{i}{j}a^{i-j}v_i$, so $W_R$ is stable under every $U^-(R)$-point. Thus $W$ is a $U^-$-submodule containing $v$, and [F4] implies $L(m)=W$. The weights $(m-2i)\chi$ are distinct, so this is a direct sum of one-dimensional spaces $kv_i$ for the nonzero coefficients; hence every weight space of $L(m)$ has dimension at most one. [F3, F4, F5]
source_lines.90: - The computation $g\cdot e_i^p=(g\cdot e_i)^p$ shows that the $p$-th symmetric power always contains the Frobenius twist $L(1)^{(p)}\cong L(p)$. For $0\le m<p$, $S^m(k^2)$ is simple: a nonzero submodule contains a weight monomial $e_1^ae_2^{m-a}$ by [F6]; the coefficient of $t^{m-a}$ in its universal $U^+$-translate is $e_1^m$, so the submodule contains $e_1^m$. The universal $U^-$-translate of $e_1^m$ has coefficients $\binom mi e_1^{m-i}e_2^i$, all nonzero because $m<p$, so the submodule is the whole symmetric power. Coefficients belong to the submodule by its coaction criterion, rather than by interpolation over $k$.
